title: Hanuman's counsel
hook: the job is done, and Hanuman could fly home, but first he holds a council with the only advisor present: himself

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hanuman's counsel, part one. The crow, the hair jewel, and none in the army weaker than me. Did you comfort someone by answering their real fear? Today, Hanuman counsels himself. Day six hundred twenty-five.
screen: `NONE IN THE ARMY WEAKER THAN ME.`

segments.voice: Mission complete. Sugriva asked for one thing, and it's done. Going home now would be perfectly fair. Or there's the other question: while I'm here, is there something more this situation needs? Hanuman has found Sita, delivered the ring, received the jewel. His mission, as Sugriva gave it, is complete. He walks a little way from Sita through the grove. And Valmiki, once again, lets us hear him think it through.

Hanuman's reasoning comes in steps. First: I've found Sita. That was the work I was given. But a little remains. Rama will have to fight Ravana. It would help him to know the enemy's strength. Second, he runs through the four classic ways of dealing with an opponent, as they're taught in Indian statecraft: conciliation, gifts, division, and force. Conciliation does no good with rakshasas, he reasons. Gifts mean nothing to those already piled with wealth. And people proud of their strength can't be split apart. So only one way is left: a show of strength, to test them and to be brought before Ravana himself. Third, he states a principle. The one fit for a task, he says, is the one who, given a job, gets many things done, without working against the first. A messenger who stops at the one thing has done only the one thing. That last clause matters. Without spoiling it. Hanuman has already secured the main thing: he's found Sita and has her jewel. Nothing he does next can undo that. Only now does he allow himself the risk. So he decides. He'll wreck this beautiful grove, Ravana's pleasure garden, to draw the rakshasas out, see how they fight, and get himself taken to Ravana. Notice the order. In the palace, despair; in the tree, careful speech; with Sita, comfort shaped to her fear. And now, with the job done, strategy. Hanuman doesn't act on impulse. He holds a council in his own head, and then he acts.
screen: `THE TASK IS DONE; A LITTLE REMAINS.` · `CONCILIATION, GIFTS, DIVISION, FORCE.` · `DO MORE, WITHOUT SPOILING IT.` · then, large: `HE DECIDES TO WRECK THE GROVE.`

segments.voice: Sit and settle. Think of a task you've recently finished. Hold it in mind, and ask yourself quietly: is there one small further thing it needs, which wouldn't put the main work at risk? A thank-you, a follow-up, a note for next time. Let the idea come or not come. Either way, breathe, and rest in the fact that the main thing is done. The bell holds the time.
Hanuman's counsel. His deliberation in the grove: the main task done, the four ways weighed, and the decision to do more, without spoiling what's been achieved.
Your line: do more, without spoiling it. Today, once a task is safely done, ask what one further step would help, and take it only if it risks nothing you've won. Day six hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Some teachers of the Sundara Kanda cite Hanuman's deliberation before destroying the grove as a model of a capable envoy, and the four means of statecraft he weighs are a standard idea in classical Indian political thought.

myth: Hanuman wrecks the grove in a burst of anger
he reasons it through step by step first.
Hanuman says the one fit for a task gets more done, without spoiling the main task
and his main task, finding Sita, is already secure.
Hanuman thinks gifts might win over Ravana
he reasons that gifts mean nothing to those already rich.

fork.setup: you're Hanuman. you've found Sita and have her jewel. your mission is done. what now?
options: test the enemy's strength and get yourself taken to Ravana.
fork.reveal: Hanuman decides that, with the main task secure, he should learn the rakshasas' strength and meet Ravana, so he begins to wreck the grove.

original.note: Sanskrit dūta, messenger or envoy: Hanuman's role in Lanka.

trapdoor: what you thought: wrecking the grove is just Hanuman showing off.
what it means: it's a deliberate strategy, chosen only once the main task is secure.

what a scholar hears: the four upāyas (sāma, dāna, bheda, daṇḍa) are a standard framework of Indian statecraft, found in texts like the Arthashastra and the Mahabharata; Hanuman applies them in miniature.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Sundara Kanda 41 (Hanuman's deliberation; the four means; the ideal messenger)

notes: Hanuman's reasoning through the four upāyas in Sundara 41: confirm that all four are named there and his reasons for rejecting each.
The principle of the ideal messenger (doing more than assigned without harming the main task): confirm wording and verse.
Arthashastra and Mahabharata as sources of the four upāyas: confirm the Keeper is comfortable naming them.

Fresh review: corrected Hanuman's reason for rejecting division (Sundara 41: those proud of strength cannot be divided, not 'one messenger can't do it tonight') and gifts (those who have amassed wealth, not 'the richest king in the world'); restated the messenger principle closer to the verse; replaced the 'end of the list' style hook, which echoed day 615.
